fields.security_summary: LPDDR5 SDRAM as defined in JESD209-5 is a commodity mobile memory device with NO confidentiality, NO authentication, NO bus-level encryption, NO access control, and NO secure erase at the protocol layer. It does provide on-the-wire data-integrity protection via Read/Write Link ECC (16-bit, single-bit correcting) and, from JESD209-5B, Adaptive Refresh Management (RFM) plus per-row activation tracking that improve reliability against Rowhammer-class disturbance. All cryptographic security — at-rest encryption, anti-replay, key management, secure boot — is layered above the LPDDR5 channel by the memory controller / SoC (e.g. ARM TrustZone-aware controllers, inline memory encryption engines in mobile application processors).

security_features_at_protocol_level.name: Link ECC (Read / Write)
security_features_at_protocol_level.scope: 16-bit link ECC over the data carried across the bus per direction.
security_features_at_protocol_level.description: Corrects a single-bit error introduced on the wire (SI / noise) in each direction. NOT a cryptographic MAC; protects transport integrity only.

security_features_at_protocol_level.name: Adaptive Refresh Management (RFM)
security_features_at_protocol_level.scope: Per-bank / per-row activation accounting with controller-issued RFM commands.
security_features_at_protocol_level.description: Mitigates Rowhammer-class bit flips by triggering targeted refresh when activation counts to aggressor rows exceed a threshold. Reliability feature, not a security/authentication primitive.

security_features_at_protocol_level.name: Permanent Write Protect (none)
security_features_at_protocol_level.description: LPDDR5 has no built-in write-protect register; all cells are writable while the addressed bank is open.

fields.no_confidentiality: The LPDDR5 bus carries plaintext data on the DQ lines. An attacker with physical bus access (probe / interposer) can sniff reads and writes in plain; cold-boot-style attacks remain a system-level concern. At-rest encryption is provided (if at all) by the SoC memory controller, not by the LPDDR5 component.
fields.no_authentication: LPDDR5 has no command authentication; any command on the CA bus (including SRE, MRW to alter mode registers, deep-sleep entry) is accepted unconditionally per the command encoding.
fields.no_access_control: LPDDR5 has no per-bank, per-row, or per-address access control at the protocol level.
fields.rowhammer_class_vulnerabilities: Like all modern DRAM, LPDDR5 is susceptible to Rowhammer-class disturbance. JESD209-5B adds Adaptive Refresh Management (RFM) and activation-count-based targeted refresh to mitigate it; full mitigation still depends on correct controller policy (refresh rate, RFM thresholds) and, optionally, system-level ECC.
fields.comparison_to_sibling_standards: DDR3 (JESD79-3) has no on-bus CRC/parity and no Rowhammer mitigation (Rowhammer was first demonstrated on DDR3). DDR4 added command/address parity, optional data-bus CRC, and TRR hooks. DDR5 added on-die ECC and Refresh Management. LPDDR5 brings link ECC (on-the-wire) and, in 5B, Adaptive Refresh Management — but, like DDR, leaves confidentiality/authentication to the controller/SoC.
fields.notes: Security at the LPDDR5 layer is intentionally minimal in JEDEC's design — JESD209-5 is a high-throughput, low-power mobile memory standard whose protocol-level protections are transport-integrity (Link ECC) and reliability (RFM), not cryptographic. Systems needing at-rest LPDDR5 encryption use a memory controller with inline encryption (transparent to the LPDDR5 component spec).
